text: Course eight gave you the real mechanics of PAM: credential vaulting, session recording, Azure PIM's eligible-and-active model for just-in-time role activation. That was usually framed around one team managing one set of roles. This lesson takes the exact same mechanisms and asks what has to change to run them across an entire enterprise instead.

The honest answer is: the mechanisms themselves don't change. Vaulting still replaces memorized passwords. JIT activation still beats standing privilege. What changes is the surface those mechanisms now have to cover — dozens of business units, multiple AD forests or Entra tenants, on-prem domain admin rights, cloud subscription owner roles across many subscriptions, and database admin access, each historically governed by whichever team happened to own that one system.

Covering that surface consistently needs two things course-eight scale never required. A role catalog gives every privileged role across the whole enterprise the same definition, so you can actually answer a question like who can read customer financial data company-wide. And segregation-of-duties checking has to run across that entire catalog, because a dangerous combination — someone who can both create a vendor and approve payments to it — is invisible to any single approver reviewing one request in isolation.

Every enterprise PAM program also needs a small number of break-glass accounts, reserved for when the approval system or identity provider itself is down and someone still needs emergency access. These sit deliberately outside the normal JIT flow — they have to, since that flow is exactly what might be unavailable. But they're not ungoverned: vaulted separately, rotated immediately after any use, and every use triggers a mandatory alert and after-action review.

The goal isn't a separate PAM program per system — it's one central policy for time-boxing, approvals, and review cadence, applied consistently across on-prem domain admin, cloud roles, and database access alike, even though the mechanics underneath each one differ. Lesson 12 pushes that same consistency one step further, into a hybrid environment where on-prem Active Directory and cloud identity have to live under that one policy model together.
